Feature: Stale-observation detection and flagging for mutable environments
Pain point: An agent's tool observations can go stale mid-task if the environment's underlying state changes (a concurrent write, a branch, a scheduled mutation), and nothing tells the agent or a reviewer that a fact it relied on is now outdated
Source dates: Concord/When Agent Context Goes Stale 2026-10-04 (v2 2026-10-06), read 2026-10-19; AMV-Guard/action-conditioned memory verification 2026-10-22 read 2026-11-02; Patronus MEMTRACK date unknown (~2025-10) read 2026-11-02 (incomplete access); Anthropic components of agent memory 2026-11-06 read directly 2026-11-16; WikiTrace / Don't Just Trust Your Memory 2026-11-10 read 2026-11-23
Label: Proposed
Differentiator angle: LayerLens environments are already deterministically versioned and mutable (mintable, branchable); a staleness flag extends that existing backend versioning to the agent-facing side, turning a property we already have into a new legible signal
Notes: New 2026-10-19, from the arXiv inbox cs.OS harvest. Dedup: checked vs I-0009 (post-failure error-message guidance, distinct) and I-0007/T-06 (environment-state lifecycle from the system side, distinct from the agent's belief about that state going stale). Single source; needs a second source or a product-check result to reach L1. | **Promoted L0->L1 2026-11-02**: a second independent source and mechanism (AMV-Guard, action-conditioned verification scaling re-check effort to the pending action's consequence) joins Concord (source-change detection); a third, adjacent source (Patronus MEMTRACK) shows agents often fail to even invoke memory tools effectively, a prerequisite problem.; 2026-11-16: +1 source (C-0149, a first-party frontier-lab admission of the exact staleness risk this feature targets); confidence/priority unchanged; 2026-11-23: +1 source (C-0168, a third distinct mechanism: evidence-linked memory lets an agent check a lesson against its own trajectory before acting on it)
In plain terms: If something an agent looked at earlier (a file, a record) changes while it is still working, flag that its information is now out of date instead of letting it keep acting on the old version. Helps separate 'the agent made a mistake' from 'the agent was working off information that changed underneath it.'
Why now: A third independent mechanism (evidence-linked self-checking) joins source-change detection and action-conditioned verification, widening the design space for how a staleness/trust flag on an environment observation could actually be resolved, not just raised.

Feature: Cross-document information-aggregation leak detection for mixed-clearance environments
Pain point: An agent's legitimate access to several individually-permitted records can combine into a disclosure none of them authorized alone (a confidentiality 'mosaic effect')
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: LayerLens's own shipped system types carry mixed-sensitivity records within one tenant; a dedicated mosaic-leak grader would be a differentiated safety check no generic observability competitor currently names
Notes: New 2026-11-02, from the discovery harvester (HF Daily Papers). Dedup: checked vs F-0009 (tool/error-surface guidance, distinct), F-0006 (consequence-naming confirmations, distinct), and the trust-wall/credential-isolation cluster under T-02 (distinct — protects secrets, not inferable conclusions from legitimately-accessed records). Single source; needs a second source or a product-check result to reach L1.
In plain terms: Check whether an agent's final answer combines facts from several individually-fine records into a conclusion that none of them, alone, would have allowed it to state. A research paper found this happens at real, non-trivial rates even with safeguards in place.
Why now: A directly-relevant paper quantifies a confidentiality failure mode LayerLens's own mixed-sensitivity system types (Salesforce, Gmail, SEC EDGAR) could plausibly exhibit, that no existing idea in the backlog addresses.

Pain point: Nothing in a typical agent memory or retrieved-content pipeline records who actually said something or with what authority, so an attacker-controlled source can get misattributed as the user's own instruction or preference
Evidence links: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38209v1; https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28093v2; https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07483; https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09721; https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07050; https://www.anthropic.com/research/components-of-agent-memory; https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12068
Source dates: Role Grounding Attack 2026-10-28 read 2026-11-09; ClawMMU 2026-10-20 (v2 2026-10-25) read 2026-11-09; Signed but Not Safe 2026-11-05 read 2026-11-16; MemoryDojo 2026-11-06 read 2026-11-16; Authorization Propagation in A2A 2026-11-04 read 2026-11-16; Anthropic components of agent memory 2026-11-06 read directly 2026-11-16; MIRIX-2.0 date unknown read 2026-11-23
Label: Proposed
Differentiator angle: Extends the trust wall's own 'the agent cannot see behind this boundary' logic from secrecy to authorship: not just hiding a secret, but refusing to let authority self-elevate
Notes: New 2026-11-09, from the arXiv inbox cs.MA harvest (a matched attack/defense pair in the same week's harvest). Dedup: checked vs F-0011/I-0011 (stale observations, about content going out of date, not about who said it) and the trust-wall/credential-isolation cluster under T-02 (about secrets staying hidden, not about authorship of non-secret content). Distinct enough to merit a new row. Two independent sources at creation (an attack paper and a structurally distinct, independently-authored defense mechanism) satisfy L1 directly.; **Promoted L1->L2 2026-11-16**: four new sources across three distinct mechanisms (signed-handoff extraction, general memory-poisoning benchmark, delegation-authority attenuation) plus a first-party Anthropic admission of the underlying risk satisfy the L2 bar (multiple independent sources, named persona, stated user outcome, open design question, concrete validation plan).; 2026-11-23: +1 source (C-0169, an architecture-level corroboration: a 'provenance hypergraph' indexing memory records that cite their originating rows); confidence/priority unchanged (already L2)
In plain terms: Make sure that if an agent remembers something (a preference, an instruction), the system also remembers who actually said it and with what authority, so an outside attacker's words can never get quietly recorded as if the real user said them.
Why now: A shipped, benchmark-leading memory architecture (MIRIX-2.0) implements close to the exact record-level provenance tracking this feature's hypothesis calls for, evidence the mechanism is not just theoretically sound but practically buildable.

Feature: Proof-based grading tier for agent-written code/plans, alongside existing Graders
Pain point: LayerLens's graders (answer/actions/judge/state) all check specific observed inputs/outcomes against an answer key or rubric — the same evidentiary category as a passing test; there is no stronger, 'holds for every input' evidence tier
Source dates: Soteria 2026-11-13 read 2026-11-23; Microsoft PDD Kit 2026-11-05 read directly 2026-11-23; EvoTrias 2026-11-13 read 2026-11-23 (supporting context)
Label: Proposed
Differentiator angle: A 'proven' verdict is a strictly stronger evidentiary claim than any of LayerLens's current Grader/Judge/Scorer outputs, directly extending the 'mechanical grading, nothing self-scored' trust story to agent-written code/plans specifically
Notes: New 2026-11-23, from two independent sources (an academic paper, Soteria, and a frontier-lab research prototype, Microsoft's PDD Kit) converging on the same test-vs-proof evidence-quality distinction in the same week, plus EvoTrias as architectural supporting context (why judging authority must stay structurally separate). Dedup: checked against existing graders (all test/rubric-shaped) and I-0014 (reviewer-facing attestation — about exposing an existing evidence chain, not creating a stronger evidence tier); distinct.
In plain terms: For the parts of a task that can be stated as a strict rule (like 'this balance must never go negative'), prove the agent's code or plan satisfies that rule for every possible input, not just the handful of cases a test happened to try. A 'proven' result is a stronger guarantee than a 'passed the tests' result.
Why now: Two independent sources (one academic, one a frontier lab's own research prototype) converged on formal, proof-based verification of agent-generated artifacts in the same week — a genuinely new, nameable evidence tier worth tracking before any competitor claims it as a differentiator.
